defaults.teacher_persona: A working data-and-AI lead who has shipped AI drafts into real teams and always shows the verification step before the shortcut.
classmates: A frontline employee who wants the time saving and is wary of being blamed for an error
A supervisor who has to sign off on the work and asks what could go wrong
defaults.interaction: Workshop-style: the teacher demonstrates one move on a real workplace artifact, then the peers attempt it on their own and compare what they caught.
defaults.assessment: Each classroom ends with 3-5 checks aligned to the chapter's graded activity.

classrooms.title: The Confident Wrong Answer
classrooms.prompt: A team has received a fluent, AI-drafted customer memo that contains two invented facts (a statistic and a policy detail). Have the AI teacher explain, in plain language, how a language model produces plausible text token by token and why fluency is not evidence, then run a draft-and-verify exercise: one classmate drafts, one checks every claim against the supplied source, one records what the draft got wrong. Include slides on prediction versus retrieval and on confabulation, a roleplay where the AI states an invented statistic confidently, and a short quiz on which claims need a source. End with a checklist learners can apply to their own AI drafts at work. Beginners, no coding.
objectives: Explain why a fluent AI answer can be wrong
Verify claims against a source before using them
Apply a short verification checklist to a workplace draft

classrooms.title: Which Tasks Get the Assistant?
classrooms.prompt: Give the class a list of ten realistic workplace tasks (meeting notes, a first-draft email, a policy answer, a customer refund decision, a training quiz, a spreadsheet formula, a performance review, a safety check). The teacher introduces a simple triage: cost of a wrong answer, reversibility, and whether a human can check the result cheaply. The classmates sort the ten tasks into use-now, use-with-review, and do-not-use, defend their choices, and revise one after hearing a counter-argument. Include slides on task fit and a simulation where a task is moved between tiers as new information arrives. Close with the triage card learners will use at work.
objectives: Sort tasks by the cost of a wrong answer
Defend and revise a task-fit decision

classrooms.title: What May Leave the Building
classrooms.prompt: Run a data-handling drill: the class is shown eight snippets (a customer email with an address, a public job posting, a sick note, an internal pricing sheet, a published report, a colleague's performance note, a contract clause, a screenshot of a spreadsheet). The teacher explains why pasted text may leave the organization and why 'delete my chat' is not a data-retention policy, then the peers classify each snippet as public, internal, confidential, or restricted and name the approved route for the confidential and restricted ones. Include a roleplay where a colleague asks the AI to summarize a restricted document, and a quiz on the employer's rule versus the tool's default. Emphasize: when unsure, stop and ask.
objectives: Classify workplace data before pasting it into a tool
State what counts as personal or restricted data
Use the approved route instead of a public chat window

classrooms.title: Build the Habit That Catches Errors
classrooms.prompt: Have the class build a personal verification routine and then stress-test it. The teacher models a four-step check (name the claims, find the source, compare, record the decision), the peers apply it to a deliberately flawed AI draft, and then the AI introduces a plausible but wrong correction while they are checking. Include slides on checking cost versus error cost, a roleplay on pushback when a manager wants to skip the check, and a short assessment where learners choose the right next step for four short scenarios. End by having each learner write the one rule they will keep.
objectives: Keep checking when the AI sounds certain
Hold the line with a manager who wants to skip review
